questions.title: Following a metal through two oxidation states
questions.stem: An aqueous first-row transition metal M has atomic number 26. A sample contains M²⁺ and M³⁺. The two ions can be separated before their absorption spectra are measured.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the noble-gas electron configurations of M, M²⁺ and M³⁺.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why the aquated ions may absorb different visible wavelengths even though the metal is the same.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A particular absorption has wavelength 510 nm. Determine the energy absorbed per mole of photons. Use h=6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s, c=3.00×10⁸ m s⁻¹ and NA=6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The M³⁺ fraction of a 1.60 mmol mixture is first reduced completely to M²⁺ using 48.25 C, with 100% current efficiency. Use Q=n(e⁻)F and F=96500 C mol⁻¹. Determine the original amount of each ion.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: A second analyst infers the original proportions from the mixed solution’s colour alone. Evaluate the inference and propose a quantitative alternative.

steps.text: M: [Ar]3d⁶4s².
M²⁺: [Ar]3d⁶, removing 4s first.
M³⁺: [Ar]3d⁵.
Ligands split the metal d orbitals into groups of different energy.
Absorption promotes an electron between available d levels, with ΔE=hf.
Oxidation state changes metal–ligand interactions and the energy separation.
Convert λ to 5.10×10⁻⁷ m.
E per photon=hc/λ=3.90×10⁻¹⁹ J.
E per mole=2.35×10² kJ mol⁻¹.
M³⁺ + e⁻ → M²⁺, so 0.500 mmol M³⁺ initially.
M²⁺ initially=1.60−0.500=1.10 mmol.
Observed colour is the mixture’s transmitted light and cannot separate overlapping absorptions by inspection.
Calibrate the pure ions at two wavelengths with different relative sensitivities.
Use the two absorbances in simultaneous additive concentration equations under the same ligand conditions.

questions.answerSummary: Use the two absorbances in simultaneous additive concentration equations under the same ligand conditions.

questions.title: Closing a magnesium oxide cycle
questions.stem: All values refer to 298 K in kJ mol⁻¹. Formation of MgO(s): −602; Mg atomization: +148; successive Mg ionizations: +738 and +1451; conversion of ½O₂(g) into O(g): +249; first and second O electron-gain enthalpies: −141 and +744.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write equations, including states, for the second ionization and each of the two electron-gain steps.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the enthalpy of lattice dissociation, making the direction of the cycle explicit.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the second electron-gain step requires energy and why this does not prevent MgO from forming exothermically.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Predict how the magnitude of the lattice dissociation enthalpy changes on replacing Mg²⁺ with Ca²⁺. Explain your reasoning.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: An analyst uses +498 instead of +249 for the oxygen atomization step. Find the analyst’s dissociation enthalpy and explain the error.

steps.text: Mg⁺(g)→Mg²⁺(g)+e⁻.
Formation of the gaseous ions from the elements requires 148+738+1451+249−141+744=3189 kJ mol⁻¹.
3189+ΔH(lattice formation)=−602, giving −3791 kJ mol⁻¹.
MgO(s)→Mg²⁺(g)+O²⁻(g): +3791 kJ mol⁻¹.
An incoming electron is repelled by the negative O⁻ ion.
Energy is needed to overcome that repulsion in the gas phase.
The large negative lattice formation term more than offsets the total gaseous-ion cost.
The charge product is unchanged.
Ca²⁺ is larger, increasing closest ion separation.
Attraction weakens; the positive dissociation enthalpy decreases.
The gaseous-ion total rises by 249 kJ mol⁻¹.
The apparent dissociation enthalpy becomes +4040 kJ mol⁻¹.
Only half a mole of O₂ is dissociated per mole of MgO.

questions.answerSummary: Only half a mole of O₂ is dissociated per mole of MgO.

questions.title: Substitution and stereochemical evidence
questions.stem: One enantiomer of 2-bromobutane reacts with water in a polar solvent. At constant solvent composition, doubling the substrate concentration doubles the initial rate. At constant substrate concentration, independently added nucleophile changes the initial rate negligibly. The substitution product has a small enantiomeric excess, defined here as the absolute difference between the percentages of the two enantiomers.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the empirical rate expression consistent with the data, give the units of k, and identify the bond broken in the slow step of the proposed unimolecular pathway.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Represent ionization and attack by water, describing the origin and destination of each electron-pair arrow.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Complete the mechanism and explain the formation of both configurations.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A sample contains 54.0% of one enantiomer and 46.0% of the other. Determine its enantiomeric excess and assess whether the data require a perfectly free carbocation.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Contrast this result with a single concerted backside displacement on the same enantiomer by OH⁻.

steps.text: Rate=k[2-bromobutane].
k has units s⁻¹.
C–Br breaks heterolytically in the rate-determining ionization.
Arrow from the C–Br bond to Br, giving Br⁻ and CH₃CH⁺CH₂CH₃.
A water oxygen lone pair points to the carbocation carbon.
Attack gives CH₃CH(OH₂⁺)CH₂CH₃.
Another water molecule accepts a proton; the oxonium O–H bond pair returns to O, giving butan-2-ol.
The approximately planar carbocation can be attacked from either face.
Attack on opposite faces gives the two enantiomers.
Enantiomeric excess=54.0−46.0=8.0%.
A completely free planar intermediate in an achiral environment would give equal access to both faces.
The small excess is consistent with unequal access, for example shielding by a departing ion; it does not require a free intermediate.
Rate=k[substrate][OH⁻] for elementary bimolecular substitution.
Bond formation and leaving-group departure occur in one step.
Backside attack gives inversion at the reacting carbon, rather than near-racemization.

questions.answerSummary: Backside attack gives inversion at the reacting carbon, rather than near-racemization.

questions.title: A shift reactor at 700 K
questions.stem: CO(g)+H₂O(g) ⇌ CO₂(g)+H₂(g). Assume ΔH°=−41.0 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS°=−42.0 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ are constant over the range considered. Use R=8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Treat the gases as ideal.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate ΔG° at 700 K and deduce whether the standard-state forward reaction is product-favoured.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the equilibrium constant and state how changing the catalyst affects it.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Starting with 1.00 mol of each reactant and no products, calculate the equilibrium amount of H₂.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A different mixture at 700 K has Q=15. Calculate the actual ΔG and predict its initial direction of net change.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Find the temperature for K=1 and explain why compressing the equilibrium gas mixture at fixed temperature does not change its composition in this model.

steps.text: ΔS°=−0.0420 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
Negative ΔG° means K>1.
A catalyst changes approach rates but leaves K unchanged at fixed temperature.
With extent x, amounts are 1−x, 1−x, x, x.
K=x²/(1−x)²; the common pressure or volume factors cancel.
x=√K/(1+√K)=0.731 mol (approximately).
ΔG=ΔG°+RT ln Q.
The reverse reaction initially predominates since Q>K.
K=1 requires ΔG°=0, so T=ΔH°/ΔS°≈976 K.
Compression multiplies all partial pressures by the same factor.
Equal gaseous stoichiometric totals on both sides leave Q unchanged at K.

questions.answerSummary: Equal gaseous stoichiometric totals on both sides leave Q unchanged at K.

questions.title: Iron content of a process sample
questions.stem: A 1.250 g process sample is dissolved without oxidizing its iron. All iron is present as Fe²⁺ in 250.0 cm³. A 25.00 cm³ aliquot consumes 20.00 cm³ of 0.02000 mol dm⁻³ MnO₄⁻ in excess sulfuric acid. M(Fe)=55.85 g mol⁻¹. E°(MnO₄⁻/Mn²⁺)=+1.51 V and E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺)=+0.77 V.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Construct the balanced overall ionic equation using half-equations.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass percentage of iron in the original sample.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine the standard cell potential and ΔG° per mole of permanganate consumed. Use F=96500 C mol⁻¹.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A small fraction of Fe²⁺ oxidizes in air during dilution. Predict the changes to titre and calculated percentage, and suggest a control.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Each burette reading has uncertainty ±0.05 cm³. Estimate the maximum percentage uncertainty from the titre and distinguish it from the oxidation error.

steps.text: MnO₄⁻+8H⁺+5e⁻→Mn²⁺+4H₂O.
Fe²⁺→Fe³⁺+e⁻.
MnO₄⁻+8H⁺+5Fe²⁺→Mn²⁺+4H₂O+5Fe³⁺.
The aliquot consumes 4.000×10⁻⁴ mol MnO₄⁻, equivalent to 0.002000 mol Fe²⁺.
The sample contains 0.02000 mol Fe, or 1.117 g.
Iron=89.36% (accept 89.4%).
Use ΔG°=−nFE°, with n=5 per mole of permanganate.
ΔG°≈−357 kJ mol⁻¹.
Oxidized Fe³⁺ does not consume permanganate as Fe²⁺ does; the titre decreases.
The apparent Fe percentage is too low.
Prepare and titrate promptly under oxygen-limiting conditions, e.g. deoxygenated solution under inert gas.
Maximum absolute uncertainty in the difference=0.10 cm³.
Reading uncertainty can affect measurements in either direction; prior oxidation biases the result systematically low.

questions.answerSummary: Reading uncertainty can affect measurements in either direction; prior oxidation biases the result systematically low.

questions.title: Identifying a volatile carbonyl
questions.stem: A neutral compound with molecular formula C₅H₁₀O shows a molecular ion at m/z 86, a strong IR absorption near 1715 cm⁻¹ and no broad O–H absorption. Its ¹H NMR spectrum has only a triplet integrating to 6H and a quartet integrating to 4H. Assume ordinary first-order splitting.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the index of hydrogen deficiency and explain which feature accounts for it.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Deduce the structure and assign both signals, including the reason for each splitting pattern.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why pentan-2-one and pentanal each fail at least one observation and why the molecular-ion peak alone cannot distinguish them.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Predict the main product of reduction of the carbonyl by a suitable hydride reagent followed by protonation. Discuss chirality.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: An unknown is proposed to be a mixture of unchanged ketone and its alcohol. Give two independent spectral observations expected for this mixture and explain why a broad O–H peak alone is insufficient.

steps.text: The IR band is consistent with C=O.
One carbonyl double bond uses the single degree of unsaturation, leaving no ring or other double bond.
Pentan-3-one: CH₃CH₂C(=O)CH₂CH₃.
Two equivalent terminal methyl groups couple to adjacent CH₂ (two neighbours), giving the 6H triplet.
Two equivalent CH₂ groups each couple to three methyl protons, giving the 4H quartet.
Pentan-2-one has an acetyl methyl singlet and lacks equivalence of two ethyl groups.
Pentanal would show an aldehydic proton signal and additional environments.
All three share the same molecular formula and nominal molecular mass.
Pentan-3-ol, CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₃.
The former carbonyl carbon is tetrahedral after reduction.
It carries two identical ethyl groups so is not stereogenic.
Residual C=O absorption supports remaining ketone.
New alcohol C–H proton environment on CH(OH) in ¹H NMR (or a distinct alcohol molecular ion at 88).
Water or another O–H-containing impurity could also cause broad O–H absorption.

questions.answerSummary: Water or another O–H-containing impurity could also cause broad O–H absorption.
